title: Choosing a partner
hookLine: the Gurus ask for respect and shared values, and no dowry
tomorrow: the wedding is tomorrow morning. what happens at the Granth?

lines: WHAT DO THE GURUS SAY TO LOOK FOR?
cards: Dating profiles let you filter by height, by job title, by income. Some aunties run the same filters out loud.
It's the mehndi night, the eve of the wedding, henna drying on Jasleen's hands, and from the next room Simran hears it: such a nice girl, marrying a man with no job.
Simran sits down next to her cousin, careful of the henna, and asks the question straight. Why him? Jasleen doesn't even look up.
He's the same person he was last Monday, she says. So the question for today: what do the Gurus say to look for?

teach.h: ANG 79: THE NAME AS MY DOWRY.
teach.b: The Sikh answer starts with what not to filter by. Guru Ram Das, on ang 79, gives a bride her own voice, speaking to her father before the wedding.
In paraphrase: dear father, give me the Name of God as my gift and my dowry. Not goods, not gold, not a price.

teach.h: REHAT: NO DOWRY, NO CASTE FILTER.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, speaks against dowry too, and asks that a match be made without regard to caste. What's left to look for is the person: respect, shared values, a life pointed the same way.
Character first. And here's a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.

The book of Proverbs, scripture for Jews and Christians, ends with a poem about a woman of worth, and in the King James Bible it says: "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."
Two traditions, each in its own words, looking past the surface to how someone lives before God.
One honest difference: Proverbs speaks of a wife as her husband and children praise her. Ang 79 is in the bride's own voice, asking for the Name instead of a dowry.
Jasleen blows on her henna. He was kind before he lost the job, she says. He's kind now.

how: Sikh families often help introduce a couple, and the Rehat Maryada asks that marriages be made without dowry and without regard to caste; the couple's consent and shared faith matter most.

o: letting the family choose by income and background
finding someone from exactly the same caste and town
looking for respect and shared values, not status

games.q: what to look for — tap the pairs.
p: the Name of God as my dowry
beauty is vain; character is praised
he's the same person he was

s: in a Sikh marriage, a dowry shows the family's respect
on ang 79 the bride asks for the Name of God as her dowry, and the Rehat Maryada speaks against dowry.
Proverbs, read by Jews and Christians, also looks past beauty to how someone lives before God
Proverbs 31:30 praises a woman that feareth the LORD over beauty. each tradition says it in its own words.
the two texts say exactly the same thing
one honest difference: Proverbs speaks of a wife as others praise her; ang 79 is the bride's own voice.

games.q: a friend is choosing between two people: one with a great job and a short temper, one between jobs and steady as a rock. what does today's teaching put first?
o: character: respect and shared values, which outlast any job.
security: a great job now protects the marriage later.
family approval: whichever one the relatives prefer.
games.why: the Gurus look past goods and status to the person. Jasleen put it simply: he was kind before he lost the job, and he's kind now.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you trust deeply, a friend, a partner, a relative. Let their job, their looks and their money fall away from the picture.
Stay with what's left: how they treat people when nobody's watching.

wordCard.voice: Choosing a partner. In Sikhi, looking for respect and shared values, with no dowry and no caste filter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daaj, dowry; on ang 79 the bride asks for the Name of God as hers.

carryVoice: Character first, the thing that's still there on the day the job isn't. The henna's dry; the wedding's at dawn.

sources.ref: Ang 79 (Sri Raag Chhant, Guru Ram Das: har prabh mere babulaa har devhu daan mai daajo), paraphrased
Sikh Rehat Maryada, on marriage (no dowry, no regard to caste)
